```text
              a push not sent after IndexPushLife on a fake clock, monotonic and wall; restart with units on
              disk; the bound; a dropped hint still leaving an erased document out
```

**Schedules.** FS-74, FS-75, FS-107 and FS-108 as 1.8 rewords them, through real engines on T2 and server's handlers on T3 (SEARCH-M10-35, SEARCH-M10-36). FS-107 runs with every cache discarded and the purge between, as now: a base lost to a reused slot shows only then.

**The explorer.** SEARCH-M10-35's seeded explorer drives the fake store with `IndexMerge.tla`'s actions (a head push in each of its four shapes, a merge, a roll-up's steps, a companion build split at each read, a restart, a tick) and checks FI-18, FI-20 and I1 after every step: ten seeds a merge on T2.

**Properties** (fuzz targets in the root): a merge is a function (any order of its inputs' files gives equal bytes); a merge of nothing but its own output changes only nothing; `plan` twice on one base and one document set gives equal bytes; every file a plan, a merge or a roll-up writes passes the canonical decoder and I1 holds on the result.

**Mutants.** Each twin of 1.3 is a mutant of the code and must fail a named test: a seal that leaves the head unwritten (R2's two-push test); a seal that reuses a kept slot, a push that removes a kept large entry and a merge that removes large entries (FS-107, caches discarded); a merge that drops a tombstone and a roll-up that reads no head (FS-108); a roll-up that drops a tombstone above a newer bucket's older entry, and one that writes the target's shard without its manifest (FS-75's promotion case); a companion build that reads content before the index or from a cached pin, and one that resends after TIME_AHEAD (the journal tests).

### 1.7 Implementation notes, task by task

Order: SEARCH-M10-45 first, since every other task plans on its `plan`. Then SEARCH-M10-10, then SEARCH-M10-11 and SEARCH-M10-12 together, SEARCH-M10-13, SEARCH-M10-14, SEARCH-M10-15, and the schedules as their mechanisms land. SEARCH-M10-46 at any time. All are the evs lane's. Entries for the two new tasks are in `.stack/plan/proposals/details-1-tasks.md`.

**SEARCH-M10-45, writer heads on own bases** (new; M). It finishes SEARCH-M10-09's draft to 1.2.2 and 1.2.3. The landed code that changes:

```text
evs_index_dependency.go   indexChooseEntry becomes 1.2.3's choose over the writer's own files and a keep set;
                          it takes no indexBucketDocuments. indexBucketDocuments.resolve and resolveDepth give
                          way to one lookup, the full entry of a key and version in a writer's other slots and
                          large entries; indexChainMaxDiffCount, indexEntryPlace and keptOutsideHeads go.
evs_index_head.go         indexPlanHead loads no shard for the push's own buckets (it still looks at newer
                          buckets for D-EVS-45's move, and only where the device holds them). indexPlaceEntries:
                          the branch "sealed as it stood" writes the old head's bytes again; takeSlot skips kept
                          slots and counts the ring over slots that are not kept; a plan gains the removals of
                          absorbed large entries that are not kept; a push past DirectBytes writes its head too.
                          indexHeadPlan.files() gains removals().
evs_index_view.go         indexViewWriter gains unabsorbed() and kept(); nothing else.
evs_index_files.go        indexValidateFile: coverage sorted by ref_id then horizon; a large entry's one entry is
                          kind 1; a diff only in a slot.
search_chains.go,         searchNewChainSources takes the diff's own writer's slots and large entries, and
search_match.go           searchResolveChain resolves in one step from them (1.2.9); absorbed slots and
                          absorbed large entries are not scanned (SEARCH-M10-23's draft resolved through the
                          bucket's shards, sealed slots and large entries, chains included)
protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md  1.8's text
testdata/index/head/      rewritten to 1.6's list
```

Traps: bases are chosen against the files as the push's base shows them, never against a slot this same push writes; the keep set is recomputed from the plan's own result, in key order, so two builds agree; the head rule holds for a push that writes only large entries and for one that merges its own entries; `indexComposeDelta` has no caller left in a writer and stays for tests of INDEX-FORMAT.md's Deltas.

**SEARCH-M10-10, bucket merges** (held; L; its Build changes). Build 1.2.4: `indexMerge` as the pure function `merge` with `layout` and `take`, and `IndexMerger` as its runner. Needs: SEARCH-M10-45 in place of SEARCH-M10-09 alone. What leaves its plan entry: heads as an input, the output row's "unless" clause, "absorbed large entries are removed", and "never drop a base a current head names", which is now the writer's keep rule. What joins it: `extra` entries and a no-absorb mode, for a push that merges its own entries and for SEARCH-M10-11's promotions; the tie order; a manifest-only commit; restart on `collected`. Proposed shapes: `indexMergeArgs{bucket *indexViewBucket, extra []*indexEntry, absorb bool, erased func(key, version) bool, padKey *indexPadKey, tables indexTables}` and `indexMergeResult{shards []*indexPlannedFile, removedShards []*indexPushRemoval, manifest *indexPlannedFile, malformed []*indexMalformedDiff}`. Barriers `evs.index.merge.built`, `.uploaded`, `.pushed`. Traps: the shard encoder is called up to 12 times by `take` when a shard fills, so `take` asks it for a length, not bytes, and the encoder must reach §11.14's 7 to 10 ns a posting first (the draft measured 843 ns under load, 1.4); on an app host the inputs stay in storage and the merge is a k-way pass over their key streams (1.4); the watermark is the highest seq read, never the head's; a merge writes no slot and removes no large entry. Tests: 1.6's merge vectors and fake-store cases; FS-74's two mergers; FS-107's and FS-108's merge clauses.

**SEARCH-M10-11, roll-ups and the index lock** (held; L; its Build changes). Build 1.2.5. `indexRollup` is pure over S whole, all, and a lookup "the newest version of this key in the newer buckets", which the runner answers from §5.9's version table where CORE-M10-02 has landed and else from a key-to-version run built in storage from the newer buckets' doc tables and slots. Step 4's in-place rewrite leaves the task: the roll-up calls `indexMerge` with `extra` and `absorb` false for each promotion target. `rewriteWithout` (landed, SEARCH-M10-05) keeps its two other callers, a CLOSURE and a DROP. Expiry is judged at the push's signed time, for the trigger, the lock and the merge runner's "never on an expired bucket"; the lock renews at half its term. `indexer_search.go` schedules merges, roll-ups and backfills as planned. Step 5's coverage rows go into the runner's own head in the newest bucket through `indexPlanHead` with no document. Traps: read S, the newer buckets and all at one head version taken after the lock commits; a 409 that is not the lock's keeps the lock and reruns from the read; a promotion writes the target's manifest even when it had none; a/m's `rolled_through_day` and I-EVS-11 as 1.8 words them. Tests: 1.6's roll-up vectors (one with a promotion replaces "one removing an older newer-bucket entry"); FS-75's barriers; the promotion races.

**SEARCH-M10-13, the in-ref writer on the real push builder** (held; L; Needs and Build change). Needs gain SEARCH-M10-45, SEARCH-M10-42 and SEARCH-M10-44: no index is written outside tests on the old extractor (section 11.5), and `Prepare` runs on phones, where extraction must be the one-pass form. It may be drafted against the whole-value extractor behind one seam and switched when SEARCH-M10-44 lands. `IndexWriter.Prepare(plan)` calls `indexPlanHead` (1.2.3) with the push's documents and adds every file and removal it returns to the statement. Conflict: a 409 naming the writer's head, or any file of its own, rereads its files and plans again, which is §11.14's "merges its delta into the winner's file" in effect; it is the same for an append and a seal. A push past DirectBytes calls `indexMerge` with its entries and commits the shards, the manifest and its head together. An in-ref push needs no pin and no life of its own: its content CAS is its fence. Dropped chunks: a version with fewer chunks than the one it replaces writes tombstones for the chunk numbers from its count up to the replaced version's count less one (section 11's interface), the replaced count taken from the replaced version's text; a device that does not hold that text and will not fetch it writes no index entry for the push, which then reads unindexed and is backfilled. Tests as planned, with R2's two-push case in both shapes.

**SEARCH-M10-14, companion pushes and the journal** (held; L; Needs and Build change). Needs gain SEARCH-M10-45 and SEARCH-M10-42; SEARCH-M10-44 reaches it through SEARCH-M10-13's seam. Build 1.2.6: `IndexJournal` (the unit log in the search component's sealed directory, its two states, the bound, `Committed(ref, version, signedTimeMs, documents)` called from section 8's settle and from a stream append's committed outcome for a version above the writer's own row and the ref's horizon, `ApplyErase` and `ApplyCut`) and `IndexCompanion` (the build in its six steps, the cadence, the flush before sleep or exit, the life). Settings: `Search.CompanionInterval` (QD-511) and `Search.JournalByteCount`. Traps: step 3's content head is read from evs, never from the replica's pin or a cache, and after step 2; t is taken before step 2 and the life is measured on the monotonic and the wall clock both; a push refused TIME_AHEAD is rebuilt, not resent; units leave the journal only on a known commit; the journal holds key sets, so it is read by stream and never whole (QD-641); a coverage row is raised even when every due unit was superseded. Tests: 1.6's journal list; §22.5's companion row; FS-74's killed writer; FS-108's ref DELETE and its late entry dropped at the pin.

**SEARCH-M10-15, settings, builds, off, rebuild and `ur evs index`** (held; L; two additions). A build ("on", migration's first build, a rebuild into i2, a site-loss rebuild) is a trailing push in R5's sense and follows 1.2.6's backfill: it reads the index, then the content at a pin, writes each latest window's documents through `indexMerge` with `extra` and older ones through `layout` on all, under the lock, and writes its own head in each bucket with the rows {R, pin, horizon true}. Two builders that hold the same pin build equal plaintext, which `take` and the tie order give. Each of its pushes in parts lives 25 min. Off removes every file of every writer in one push, heads included, so R2 holds without more. Everything else in its entry stands.

**SEARCH-M10-35, FS-74, FS-75 and FS-79** (held; L; cases added). FS-74 gains: one sidecar's two pushes, one appending and one sealing, of which one gets 409; a merge landing between a writer's diff and its base's absorption, the base still read; a writer's return removing its absorbed large entries. FS-75 gains: a roll-up that promotes, killed at each barrier, with a merge of the target racing it in both orders; a roll-up whose signed time is before the expiry, refused by reproducers. Its seeded explorer is 1.6's. FS-79 is unchanged but for builds following R5.

**TEST-M10-02, FI-18 to FI-24** (held; L; three checks added). `fault.FI(18)` also holds I1 on every listing it reads (every diff in an unabsorbed slot has its base in its writer's files) and I4 (all's row of a key is never above the newest bucket entry of that key), both from the canonical decoder's output and neither from index code. `fault.FI(20)` counts a promoted entry as moved: the bucket's files leave only in the push that commits all, or the target bucket's shards, holding their postings. Mutants added to its list: a merge that removes a large entry a head rests on; a roll-up that drops a tombstone above an older entry of a newer bucket; a companion push built from a pin read before the index.

**SEARCH-M10-46, IndexRollup.tla on section 1's rules** (new; M). The lane's model keeps what `IndexMerge.tla` leaves out, the erasure's CUT, CLOSUREs and epoch, and takes this section's rules for the rest: own bases with the keep rule, R2, a merge that reads no head, promotion, the pin. Its four question constants go. Its `HeadCommit` stops checking the bucket's manifest (1.1 F). §22.8's model row and `sidecartest/model/modelled.yml` name `details/IndexMerge.tla` beside it.

**Tasks not held that this touches.**

- SEARCH-M10-09 is drafted; SEARCH-M10-45 finishes it.
- SEARCH-M10-12 (coverage and backfill; it waits on SEARCH-M10-10): the backfill is 1.2.6's, with h and its two rows; `indexCoverageOf` reads up to two rows a ref; a push whose documents were all superseded is covered by its committer's next row; "re-enter a broken chain's version" becomes "re-enter a document whose diff has no base".
- SEARCH-M10-18 (DROP rewrites): a rewrite that removes a base from a writer's file removes the diffs that name it, enters a kept head's composed version full in the signer's own head, and replaces that writer's head and the bucket's manifest in the same push (1.2.3).
- SEARCH-M10-17 (erasure's rewrites): unchanged. Its list still names "each writer's slots and large entries in each bucket"; kept and lingering files are among them. A CLOSURE needs no head rewrite (1.2.3).
- SEARCH-M10-21 (reproduction): a head is reproduced from 1.2.8's inputs; hosts with the text add 1.5's check for a live entry of a removed path.
- SEARCH-M10-23 and SEARCH-M10-24 (matching and masks): 1.2.9; the reader half is in SEARCH-M10-45.
- SEARCH-M10-36 (FS-76, FS-107, FS-108): FS-107 and FS-108 as 1.8 rewords them.
- SEARCH-M10-02 is drafted; SEARCH-M10-46 brings its model to these rules.

### 1.8 Proposed DESIGN.md text

**§11.14, Files and format.** The slot row: after "a newer one replacing the writer's older one there" add "; a slot other than the head, or a large entry, at or below its writer's absorbed seq holds nothing but the bases of diffs". The entry row: for "diff: added and removed key sets against its base's set (commit path's dependency row)" read "diff: added and removed key sets against its base's set, the full entry of its key at the base version in another slot or a large entry of its own writer in its bucket (commit path's dependency row); only in a slot". The large row: add "; a full entry; its writer removes it once it is absorbed and no diff rests on it". The caps row: for "a writer holds at most 16 slots in a bucket" read "a writer holds at most 16 slots in a bucket, at most 8 of them kept for the diffs that rest on them and 8 others".

**§11.14, Commit path, the dependency row.** Replace it: "dependency a diff for version v names its base by version and rests on a full entry of its document in another file of its own writer in its own bucket: a slot that is not the head, absorbed or not, or a large entry; the newest such entry below v is the base and the delta is taken against it, so no diff rests on a diff, on a head, on a shard or on any file another device writes; a diff is written only where the delta is under half the base's set and the entry within 8 KiB, the document is no creation, and the base's slot is kept or fewer than 8 are; anything else is full; a writer keeps a file a diff of its unabsorbed slots rests on: it does not reuse such a slot nor remove such a large entry, and it removes its other absorbed large entries at its next push in the bucket; every push that writes a file of a writer's in a bucket replaces that writer's head there at the version its base showed, a head sealed as it stood written again with its own bytes, so a writer's pushes commit one at a time; a DROP's rewrite of a writer's file does the same and removes the diffs resting on what it removed (drop, below); an erasure removes a document's entries together".

**§11.14, Commit path, the seal row.** For "the lowest k whose seq the bucket's manifest shows absorbed, else a new k up to 8" read "the lowest k that the bucket's manifest shows absorbed and that is not kept (dependency, above), else a new k, up to 8 slots that are not kept".

**§11.14, Commit path, the companion row.** Replace from "each entry is encoded when its head push is built" to "as a backfill's is" with: "a companion push is built in one order: its signed time taken, the head of ur/index read, then each content ref's head read from evs, the pin; it carries, per document of the committer's journaled versions at or below the pin, the newest, and drops one whose path the content ref holds at the pin at a higher version or removed, or whose ref was deleted since, leaving the newer version to its own committer or a backfill, and one whose push a horizon row already reaches; its coverage names the pin; it is sent within 5 min of its signed time and otherwise built again, and never sent again as built after a 429 TIME_AHEAD". The conflict row: for "only an eraser's CLOSURE, a DROP's rewrite, a roll-up's step 4 or the writer's own other push rewrites a head" read "only an eraser's CLOSURE, a DROP's rewrite or the writer's own other push rewrites a writer's file".

**§11.14, Commit path, the coverage row.** After "backfills a push still unindexed 10 min after its commit into its own head and raises its horizon": "from the content at a pin read as a companion push reads it, each path at its state there; a path changed again after the horizon is left to that change's own entry". Strike "holding the buckets and all current at its push's base, dropping superseded entries (companion, above)".

**§11.14, Merges.** The input row: "input the bucket's manifest and shards, and its sealed slots and unabsorbed large entries, at the merge's base version, with the files of each writer that their diffs rest on; no head; the new manifest's absorbed seqs and the files the push replaces name them, so a reproducer learns its inputs from the push". The output row: "output each document's newest version among the inputs, each diff composed onto its base, and the erasure set's documents left out (commit path's epoch row); at one version a tombstone, then the shards' own entry, then the copy from the lowest writer id and seq; a live version as a doc-table row with its postings, a tombstone in the tombstone table, dropping the bucket's older rows of its key, and a ref tombstone those of its ref below its version, each kept for older partitions until the roll-up; appended in doc_key order to the youngest shard, which takes the longest run that fits by INDEX-FORMAT.md's search, a next one opening at the cap, its older version dropped from the shard holding it, so a bucket's shards hold one version per document, a row or a tombstone; adjacent shards under 512 KiB together are joined; a merge writes and removes no file of any writer's: slots stay for their writers to reuse, and large entries for their writers to remove". The commit row: for "the shards (uploads with receipts), the manifest and the removals" read "the shards (uploads with receipts) and the manifest, which every merge replaces or creates".

**§11.14, Roll-up.** The steps row, step 4, from "an entry of a newer bucket below a version or tombstone this roll-up carries" to "every tombstone then goes, nothing older remaining": "a version or tombstone this roll-up carries, whose document a newer bucket holds only at older versions, which racing index pushes near a boundary can leave, goes instead into the shards of the newest bucket holding an entry of it, in the same push, which replaces or creates that bucket's manifest, and stays there until that bucket rolls; a promoted tombstone still takes all's row; a ref tombstone above a newer bucket's older entry of its ref likewise; every other tombstone then goes". Step 6: for "the shards and rewrites" read "the shards, each promotion's shards and manifest, the runner's own head in the newest bucket where it carries forward, as a horizon row at indexed_through, the coverage that the removed bucket's slots held". The trigger row: add "judged at the push's signed time, as is the lock". The one row: for "with step 4, every all row is older than each bucket entry of its key and each bucket's ref tombstone of its ref, so all holds no tombstone" read "with step 4, no all row is newer than the newest bucket entry of its key, nor above a bucket's ref tombstone of its ref, so all holds no tombstone". The cost row: for "rarely, one newer bucket's file rewritten" read "rarely, one newer bucket's youngest shard and manifest rewritten".

**§11.14, Reads.** The chains row: "chains a diff resolves in one step, by its doc_key and base version in another slot or a large entry of its own writer in its bucket; a shard row of that key at that version is the same set; an unabsorbed diff whose base no such file holds, or whose composed set's size is not the diff row's trigram count, breaks the format: index_malformed names its signer, the document reads not yet searchable in coverage, never no match, and a host with the text re-enters that version full, as a backfill". The plan row: for "heads and unmerged slots are scanned per document, whose key set or composed diff chain" read "heads, sealed slots and unabsorbed large entries are scanned per document, whose key set or composed diff". The newest row: for "every all row being older than each bucket entry of its key (roll-up's one row)" read "no all row being newer than the newest bucket entry of its key (roll-up's one row)". The reproduce row: for "(the new manifest's absorbed seqs and the files the push replaces name them, the ref's listing there a merge's heads)" read "(the new manifest's absorbed seqs and the files the push replaces name them)", and after the team directory's sentence: "any writer's head is rebuilt alike from that writer's files in the bucket at the push's base and the documents the push carries: an in-ref push's content changes, or for a companion push or a backfill the paths its coverage rows name (1.2.8 of DESIGN-DETAILS.md)". The coverage row gains: "and check each live entry against its path: one whose content ref holds the path removed or at a higher version, with nothing above it in the index, is index_mismatch against its signer, and the host backfills what is missing".

**§11.14, What the server sees, the shape row.** For "rarely with one newer bucket's file rewritten in place (roll-up's step 4)" read "rarely with one newer bucket's shard and manifest rewritten (roll-up's step 4)".

**§11.14, the drop row.** After "padded to the replaced length as erase's rewrite is, with no ERASE or CLOSURE flag": "; where it takes a base from a writer's file it takes the diffs resting on it too, and replaces that writer's head and the bucket's manifest in the same push".

**§11.15, the index entries row.** "Index entries per push | proportional to the changed text where a full entry of the document sits in another of the writer's own files in the bucket (a sealed slot, or a large entry), else the document's whole key set: a writer's first entry of a document in a bucket, and each edit until the head holding it seals; a 1 MiB document per changed chunk of a large file (11.14)".

**§11.17.** D-EVS-46: for "A diff rests only on its document's previous version outside every head in the current bucket, or carries over the base of the writer's own head diff it replaces, and merges keep a base a head names" read "A diff rests only on a full entry of its document in another file of its own writer in its bucket, which that writer keeps while the diff needs it; every push that writes a writer's file replaces that writer's head". Its why gains: "a base in a file another device rewrites cannot be fenced by a push that writes only a head (DESIGN-DETAILS.md section 1)". D-EVS-47: for "a merge's writers' heads included" read "a merge reading no head"; for "and removing any older entry racing pushes left in a newer bucket" read "and moving a version or tombstone above an older entry that racing pushes left in a newer bucket into that bucket's shards". D-EVS-49: after "with coverage": ", built from the content ref as read after the index and sent within 5 min".

**§11.8, I-EVS-11.** For "the push that removes an expired bucket adds its documents to all" read "the push that removes an expired bucket adds each of its documents to all or, for one a newer bucket holds only older entries of, to that bucket's shards". A new invariant after I-EVS-17: "I-EVS-18 every diff in a slot no merge has absorbed has its base, a full entry of its document, in another file of its own writer in its bucket".

**§11.21, the risk row** "A diff's base or a deletion's mask leaves the index before the entries relying on it": its mitigation becomes "11.14's dependency row (own bases, the head rule), merges that read no head, the roll-up's promotion and the companion push's pin; an unabsorbed diff with no base is `index_malformed`; FS-107, FS-108, IndexRollup.tla and details/IndexMerge.tla".

**§22.8, FI-18.** After "since every diff's chain and every tombstone a result needs stays in the committed index": ", a diff's base in a file its own writer keeps (I-EVS-18)". **FI-20.** For "the bucket's files leave the index only in the push that commits all holding their postings" read "the bucket's files leave the index only in the push that commits all, or for a promoted document a newer bucket's shards, holding their postings".

**§22.8, FS-74.** After "one commits, the other gets 409, and its index code merges its delta into the winner's file and retries, losing and duplicating nothing": ", whether both append or one seals the head". **FS-75.** After "a window change applies from the next bucket (§11.14), every document staying searchable": "; a roll-up carrying a tombstone or a version above an older entry in a newer bucket writes it into that bucket's shards with its manifest, a merge of that bucket racing it in both orders, one of the two getting 409; a roll-up signed before its bucket's expiry is index_mismatch at every reproducer".

**§22.8, FS-107.** Replace the row's body: "diff dependency (11.14's dependency, merges and chains rows), every cache discarded before each search, the purge and evacuation run between: D created and edited twice in one unsealed head (each full entry replacing the last), then, the head sealed, edited again (a diff on the sealed slot), small and large (a large entry, then diffs on it); a fresh phone holding only the current index searches an unchanged trigram and each added and removed one; again after a merge absorbs the slot holding the base, the writer keeping that slot through three more seals and reusing it only once no diff rests on it; with each edit by another writer, each writing its own full entry once and then diffs; a merge landing between a diff's build and its commit, and a backfilled full copy of D's version beside the diff: both read, the base still there; the writer's two pushes on one base, one appending a diff and one sealing: one gets 409; a DROP listing the base takes the diff with it and writes the kept head full; a ninth kept slot is not taken and the entry is full; a forged diff whose base no file of its writer holds raises index_malformed and reads not yet searchable until a host with the text re-enters it, never no match; no body is fetched, and every search equals SearchOracle's".

**§22.8, FS-108.** For "searches mask the newer bucket's older entry, and the older bucket's roll-up removes it, rewriting its file in place" read "searches mask the newer bucket's older entry, and the older bucket's roll-up writes the tombstone into the newer bucket's shards, where it masks that entry until that bucket rolls". For "a late companion entry below an indexed version is dropped" read "a late companion entry whose document its content ref holds removed or at a higher version is dropped at the pin, with the tombstone's bucket already rolled up and nothing of the document left in the index".

**§22.8, the model row.** `details/IndexMerge.tla` beside `IndexRollup.tla`: "own bases and the head rule, merges, promotion and the pin, with §11.14's rules as written as failing configurations".

**protocol/INDEX-FORMAT.md** (SEARCH-M10-45 writes it). Entries: after "A diff's base version is below its version, and no key is in both of its sets": "A diff stands only in a slot. Its base is the full entry of its key at its base version in another file of the same writer and bucket: a slot that is not that writer's head, or a large entry; of two, the one in the file with the higher seq." Deltas: "Format 1's writers take every delta against the base itself, so nothing composes two deltas; the rule stands for readers of a later format." Slots and large entries: "A large entry's one entry is full." and, for "`coverage` is strictly ascending by ref_id", "`coverage` ascends by ref_id, then horizon false before true, with at most one row of each a ref." Shards gains `take` and the join as 1.2.4 has them, and the tie order. Small files: "`absorbed` holds a row for each writer with a watermark above 0; a manifest may list no shard." Times: "An entry's time is that of the content push that made its version; its bucket follows the signed time of the index push that carries it."

Nothing server-visible changes: no column, key, object family or proto field (I-18), and §2.8's evs-26 keeps its words but for the shape row's phrase above.

### 1.9 Owner questions

Each is filed under `.stack/questions/`, and the design above is built on its recommendation.

**Where a diff's base lives (`details-1-own-bases.md`).** §11.14 puts a diff's base in a shard or in any writer's sealed slot, which merges rewrite and absorb. The rule as written fails twice (B and D of 1.1), its patches twice more (E), and a DROP in flight is a hole no rule covers (G). Options: (1) a diff rests only on a full entry in its own writer's other files, which that writer keeps, with the head rule: no cross-device dependency is left, a merge reads no head, and `index_malformed` can no longer fall on an honest writer; it costs one full entry from each writer for each document it edits in a bucket, up to 8 kept slots (128 KiB) a writer a bucket that outlive their absorption, large entries that wait for their writer's next push, and a change to SEARCH-M10-09's and SEARCH-M10-23's drafts; (2) keep shard and sealed bases and take the questions' first options with the further patches the model asks for: no landed code changes, but `IndexMergeWritten-Patched` fails as worded and `IndexMergeWritten-PatchedTwice` with the next patch, a DROP in flight and step 4 need rules of their own, each new kind of index push must be proved against every writer's heads again, and the honest-writer alarm stays reachable; (3) no diffs: every edit writes its document's whole key set, 1.9 to 3.5 KiB against about 100 B for the source files measured, some 20 to 30 times the merge traffic of an edited repo. Recommended: 1.

**What a roll-up does about an older entry in a newer bucket (`details-1-promotion.md`).** Options: (1) promotion (R4): the carried version or tombstone moves into the newer bucket's shards and its manifest is replaced; nothing is rewritten in place, no writer's file is touched, and a late older entry is still masked for as long as that bucket lives; it costs that bucket's youngest shard and manifest, and I-EVS-11's last clause and FI-20 gain "or a newer bucket's shards"; (2) question rollup-merge-race's option 1: keep the in-place rewrite and replace the newer bucket's manifest: fewer words change, but the roll-up still deletes from writers' heads and slots, must replace each such writer's head as well (R2), conflicts with every one of those writers in flight, and removes entries without asking whether a newer diff rests on them (H of 1.1); on the model's one-document ground it passes (`IndexMergeProbe-RaceFenced`); (3) merges read older buckets and drop what they supersede (that question's option 2): phones that merge do not hold older buckets' files. Recommended: 1.

**What keeps a late entry below a dropped tombstone out (`details-1-late-entries.md`).** No push can fence a content ref and an index ref together, so no CAS closes C of 1.1. Options: (1) R5: the content pin read after the index, IndexPushLife, and never resending a stored push, with hosts holding the text repairing what a broken client gets through; it rests on evs's 10 min time check and on an expired bucket being at least a window old, and it leaves one residual: a device whose clock ran about a week fast, that stalls that long and sends stored bytes (1.5); no server change; (2) evs bumps a head counter at every roll-up and refuses index pushes built before it, as `index_epoch` does for a CUT: exact with no timing argument, but a new server rule and a new 409 for every writer in flight at each roll-up, in a design that keeps evs blind to the index (owner decision 157; D-EVS-66's "an opaque counter" was accepted once, for erasure); (3) all keeps tombstones (that question's option 3): about 25 B a deleted document for good, phones keeping only the buckets would still need them, and I-EVS-11's "all holds no tombstone" goes. Recommended: 1, with 2 held as the fallback if the review phase wants the residual closed.

**How many shards a merge may rewrite (`details-1-superseded-rows.md`).** §11.14 has a merge drop a document's older row "from the shard holding it", so a merge rewrites every shard that holds an older version of a document it carries, and a roll-up every all shard likewise. For mail that is the youngest shard alone. For an edited repository it is nearly every shard of the bucket at every merge (1.4). This section keeps the rule, since it is the design's and not one of the four counterexamples. Options: (1) keep it, as designed here: one version of a document in a bucket's shards (I-EVS-11), an eraser finds a document in one shard, and the cost of 1.4's third and fourth rows; (2) leave a superseded row where it is, masked by version, and rewrite a shard only when under half its rows are current: a merge then writes the youngest shard and little else, at the price of up to twice the bucket's bytes on every device, an eraser listing every shard that holds a version, and I-EVS-11's bucket clause; it reaches into the erasure's bounds (owner decision 146), which this section does not own. Recommended: 1 now, and 2 measured in the review phase on FS-76's corpus before M10's exit freezes the bytes.

**Small readings (`details-1-small-readings.md`).** Fourteen readings that change no D- item, listed there by number: a bucket is expired, for a merge, a roll-up and the lock, at the push's signed time; an absorbed slot or large entry holds nothing but bases; a manifest may exist with no shard and lists only writers with a watermark; coverage rows sort by ref_id then horizon, one of each a ref; an entry's time is its content push's, its bucket its index push's; a merge's tie order at one version; `take`'s search; a merge that changes nothing but watermarks still commits; a push past DirectBytes writes its head; the lock renews at half its term; a companion push that only raises coverage is sent; a writer that cannot count a replaced version's chunks writes no entry for that push; a roll-up carries the rolled bucket's coverage forward as a horizon row in its runner's head; a journaled unit at or below its ref's horizon is dropped as covered. Options: accept all, or correct any by number. Recommended: accept all.

**Existing questions this section answers.**

- `search-m10-07-keep-base-full-copy`: none of its options. Its option 1 is run as `KeepBase = "any"` and fails with merge-stale-diff's first option, as worded and widened (E of 1.1). The base moves into its own writer's files (R1), which is its option 2's aim, reached without reading other writers' heads.
- `search-m10-07-merge-stale-diff`: none of its options. Under R1 and R2 a merge's inputs always compose (I2), so the question has no case left.
- `search-m10-07-rollup-merge-race`: the fence of its option 1, the newer bucket's manifest, on a different step 4 (R4, the second question above).
- `search-m10-07-late-journal-tombstone`: its option 1, made exact: the pin is read from evs after the index, in the push's own build, and the push has a life (R5, the third question above).
- `plan-SEARCH-no-document-pushes` (QD-209), `plan-SEARCH-shrink-claim` (QD-173), `plan-SEARCH-small-readings` #4 and #6 (QD-406, QD-511), `plan-SEARCH-index-format-bytes` (QD-300) and `plan-SEARCH-sync-before-search` (QD-048): stand. QD-173's partition-keeping rewrite loses one of its three callers, the roll-up's step 4. QD-477's slot order and QD-475's paths are used as they are.

## 2. Storage consistency under stalled writes: segment GC and the MinIO settle rules (§11.13, §19.6)

Status: complete (2026-11-10)

Tasks held until complete: EVSB-M10-01, EVSB-M10-02, EVSB-M2-12, EVSB-M2-17.

Models: `sidecar/sidecartest/model/details/Settle.tla` (the store's settle rules) and `EvsGc.tla` (segment GC beside evacuation), their configurations and `run-settle.sh` beside them. Questions filed: `.stack/questions/details-2-orphan-age.md`, `.stack/questions/details-2-conditional-delete.md`, `.stack/questions/details-2-list-whole.md`, `.stack/questions/details-2-drop-job-new-ref.md`. Questions this section answers, each on the option 2.9 names: `evs-models-gc-unfenced-new-ref`, `evs-models-settle-stalled-deletes`, `evs1-m2-12-first-commit-gc-fence`, `evsb-m2-11-pending-record-no-head`.

### 2.1 The problem

§19.6's settle row (D-OPS-20) promises that a PUT or DELETE "takes effect before every later request on its key or never", and everything evs deletes rests on it: a removal marker's collection, the versionless purge, a drop job, evacuation and orphan GC all issue unconditional DELETEs. The row also admits what makes that hard. A drive commit is a check and then a rename, and one that stalls after its check lands whenever its host wakes. A write that reached N/2 + 1 drives releases its key while its other commits are still on their way. A write that fell short is reverted drive by drive, some of those reverts after its key was released.

A *stalled write* in this section is a write some of whose drive commits passed their check and have not renamed. It has one of three fates. If it already holds a write quorum it is acknowledged, and the stalled commits only add copies later. If it cannot reach one and enough drives may still hold it, it holds its key, and every request on the key waits, then fails 503, until its hosts answer. Otherwise it is released as failed and its late commits land on an unheld key. evs sees the second fate as a head it can neither read nor write, and the model `EvsCommit.tla` keeps it as `heldBy`.

TLC finds the design wrong in two places, and working them out found three more.

**A. Segment GC does not fence a ref that has no head yet (question evs-models-gc-unfenced-new-ref).** §11.13's orphans row deletes a segment no committed push introduced once it is 25 h old, after raising "the fence of each ref of the repo whose head was written before that LastModified + 24 h", waiting the store's deadline and checking the repo's commits again. A fence is a head CAS, so a ref with no head gets none. The trace, on `EvsCommit.tla` at depth 18 and on this section's `EvsGcWritten-NewRef` in 15 states:

1. A client uploads segment s1 and signs a push that creates a path on a ref never written. Its receipt is fresh.
2. evs reads the ref's head, which is absent, checks the push (5h passes: the receipt is under 24 h old), writes its batch record and issues step 7, the head created If-None-Match.
3. The PUT's drive commits stall after their checks. It holds the head's key.
4. 25 h pass. GC lists s1, finds no committed push introducing it, and lists the repo's refs to fence. The new ref has no head, so GC sends that key nothing and never learns it is held.
5. GC waits the deadline and checks the repo's commits again: none.
6. The stalled PUT lands. The head now exists, at version 1, naming s1.
7. GC deletes s1. A committed head names a deleted segment: I-EVS-1 and I-EVS-5 are broken.

On a ref with a head the same push is safe, because GC's fence CAS on that head waits behind the held key and then changes the ETag. A process paused between its last clock check and its send (FS-59's schedule) reaches the same end on a new ref without any stalled drive.

The landed evacuation meets the same wall from the other side (question evsb-m2-11-pending-record-no-head). §11.13 resolves a pending batch record by raising its ref's fence, and `HeadStore.RaiseFence` answers `ErrEvsHeadAbsent` for a ref with no head, so every push that created a ref, passed step 5 and died before step 7 leaves a record evacuation can never settle. Its minute directory stays on NVMe, and after 1,440 such minutes a run stops looking further.

**B. Two DELETEs on one key break FI-30 (question evs-models-settle-stalled-deletes).** Rule (3) releases a failed write "once the drives that may still hold it ... number under N/2, so that write can never be read". That is true of a PUT, whose version is its own. Every DELETE leaves a drive in the same state, the key absent, and a read counts absent drives together whichever DELETE left them.

*B1, stalled DELETE commits add up* (`SettleWritten-Sum`, 12 states, 4 drives on 2 hosts, read at 2). DELETE w1 takes the key, its commit on drive 1 passes its check and stalls, its deadline passes, and w1 is released as failed with one drive possibly holding it. Drive 1's commit lands: the key is absent there. DELETE w2 does the same on drive 2. Host 2 goes down. Drives 1 and 2 answer not found, a read quorum, so a GET answers 404 for a key whose acknowledged state is the initial PUT. At 8 drives two DELETEs stalling three commits each leave six drives without the key and no host need fail. Rule (3) bounds each write's stalled commits and never their sum.

*B2, a late revert undoes a later DELETE* (`SettleWritten-Revert`, 16 states at 4 drives; found at 8 drives by simulation in the question). DELETE w1 fails as above and is released; its stalled commit lands on drive 1. DELETE w2 takes the key and counts drive 1, which lacks the key, as committed, as rule (2)'s "or its absence" reads and the build does. w1's coordinator, reverting "as it lands", restores drive 1: the check passes, because the drive still lacks the key, which is all a DELETE leaves to compare. w2 commits on drives 2 and 3 and is acknowledged at three drives counting drive 1. The drives hold `initial, absent, absent, initial`: a read quorum holds the value w2's acknowledged DELETE removed.

**C. A PUT's last commit undoes a later DELETE, found here** (`SettleWritten-Straggler`, 21 states, one PUT and one DELETE, no fault). PUT w1 creates the key: three of four drives commit, w1 is acknowledged and its key released, as rule (3) says ("a later commit of it only adds a copy"), with drive 4's commit still on its way, inside its deadline. DELETE w2 takes the key. It removes the key from drives 1 and 2 and counts drive 4, which lacks it. w1's commit now reaches drive 4. Rule (2) asks whether the drive still holds what w1's coordinator read there, which was the key's absence, and it does. The commit lands. w2 is acknowledged. The drives hold `absent, absent, w1, w1`, and a GET returns the object w2 deleted. This needs a DELETE served within the deadline of a PUT on the same key, which evs's own margins keep apart (a fold's write deadline ends before a marker's collection may delete; a purge waits 60 s), but FI-30 is stated for the store, and §10.6's and later callers' margins are not evs's. It is the same defect as B2 seen from the other side: rule (2) compares the version a drive holds, and absence is not a version. A drive that lacked the key, gained it and lost it again cannot be told from one nothing touched. A heal's copy fails the same way (`SettleWritten-Heal`, 22 states): a heal reads a drive that lacks the key, a DELETE counts that drive, and the heal's commit then lands the deleted object there, which FI-30's "no heal undoes" forbids.

**D. A second GC run deletes a segment uploaded again, found here** (`EvsGcWritten-Zombie`, 18 states, no stalled write). Orphan GC's DELETE is unconditional, as every DELETE is (§11.3: MinIO ignores a condition on one), and a segment's key is its content's hash. Two GC runs decide on one orphan: taskworker's once key keeps one run per shard, but a worker paused past its claim's 5 min lease wakes beside its successor. The first run deletes the segment. Its uploader, resuming a push days later, stores the same bytes again, gets a fresh receipt and commits. The second run, still holding its decision, issues its DELETE, which takes the new object. Neither fences nor checks help, since the second run's were all made before the re-upload. The drop job is protected from this by its lease and the deadlines on its DELETEs (§11.13's clock row), marker collection by its window; orphan GC has neither.

**E. A LIST that drops a key, found here.** §11.13 deletes on what a LIST shows: a segment no pidx/ entry introduces, a container no entry names. This section adds one more, the oldest batch a LIST of pb/ returns. MinIO asks the drives of a set that are online and lists a key only if half of those hold it (`cmd/metacache-set.go:728-733`), so with three of a set's eight drives offline it can leave out a batch or an entry that five drives took and that a read would still return. No model here holds this one; it is a count of drives, in 2.2.2.

The requirement: no committed head ever names a deleted segment; FI-30 holds for every mix of PUTs and DELETEs; and the settle rules stay correct with stalled drive commits, reverts as they land, DELETEs and new refs together, inside the cost and latency §11.13 and §19.6 budget.

### 2.2 The design

#### 2.2.1 The principle

Two rules, one for each side.

**In the store, a drive commit is a compare-and-swap on what the drive has applied, and nothing of a failed DELETE outlives its key's release.** Rule (2) gains a *stamp*: each drive counts the commits it applies, and a commit lands only if none was applied to its key on that drive since its coordinator read it under the key's lock. Absence then has an identity, so a commit from before a DELETE can no longer match the absence that DELETE left (C), and a DELETE may go on counting a drive that lacks the key. Rule (3) holds a failed DELETE's key until every drive commit of it has answered and each that landed is reverted, so no two failed DELETEs' leavings are ever visible together (B1) and no revert of one runs beside a later write (B2). A PUT keeps rule (3) as written, since its version is its own.

**In evs, GC waits for evacuation instead of fencing.** Every head write that can make a segment reachable is preceded by a batch record (§11.8's steps 6 and 7), and evacuation settles every record before its batch goes: a committed one is kept behind a pidx/ entry that names the segments it introduced, and a pending one has its ref fenced and is then dead. So the oldest batch left on a cluster is a *horizon*: every push whose record is older has committed, visibly, or never will. GC deletes a segment only once the horizon has passed the last minute a receipt for it could have been checked in. It raises no fence, reads no batch and never needs the name of a ref. The one fence left is evacuation's, per pending record, and for a ref with no head that fence is a placeholder head, which §11.8's first row already has for refusals. GC's DELETE names the object it listed, so a run that wakes late deletes nothing else (D).

The push route does not change. §11.8's first commit to a new ref stays If-None-Match, with no write before step 4.

#### 2.2.2 The store: rules (2) and (3), a DELETE that names its object, and a LIST that is whole

Rules (1), (4), (5) and (6) stand as §19.6 has them. All of this is in the `minio` fork.

**Rule (2), the stamp.** Each drive's host keeps, per drive and in memory:

```text
boot       16 random hex digits, drawn when the process opens the drive
counter    how many commits the process has applied on the drive, over all keys
remembered per key, the counter's value n at the last commit applied to it, kept StampKeep (2 min) past
           that commit; keyed by the 64-bit hash the stash already uses, so two keys may share an entry,
           which can only make a commit stale
stamp      boot:n for a remembered key, boot:0 for any other
```

```text
SettleRead(key) -> version@stamp          a new storage call, under no lock (reads take none, as today)
  version   what the key's xl.meta holds, as settleVersionOf names it today, or absent, or corrupt
  stamp     read after the version

a drive commit carrying {id, expect, deadline}: a data or metadata rename, a DELETE, a heal, a revert
  arrive    stale if the id is fenced                                                        (as today)
  lock      the drive's lock on the key, held to the end; stale at the deadline              (as today)
  check     stale unless SettleRead(key) = expect; a revert checks instead that the drive still
            holds its write: the version's settle id, or the DELETE's stash with the key as that
            DELETE left it                                                                   (as today)
  gate      stale at or past the deadline, while the clock is unsure, or if the id was
            fenced meanwhile                                                                 (as today)
  mark      counter += 1; remember {key, counter, now + StampKeep}                           (new)
  rename    apply. A DELETE of a key the drive lacks applies nothing, leaves its empty stash,
            counts as committed and is marked like any other
  unlock
```

A commit that answers stale changes nothing and marks nothing. A coordinator fixes a commit's deadline before it issues the `SettleRead` whose answer the commit carries, and no deadline is more than `RequestDeadlineMax` (1 min) past its request's arrival or `CommitDeadline` (40 s) past its start, so every commit's deadline is at most 1 min after its read. The build refuses to start unless `StampKeep` is at least twice the larger of the two.

The stamp is compared whole, as a string, so a restart, which draws a new boot, makes every commit read before it stale: rule (5) already keeps the old process's commits off the drive. A drive's version and stamp are read without the drive's lock, so a read beside a commit can pair the old version with the new stamp or the new with the old. Such a pair is the drive's state once that commit ends, or never is while the commit's entry is remembered, since the counter only rises; and 2.3 shows a forgotten entry can only be matched by a commit past its deadline.

**Rule (3), a DELETE.** The coordinator's states for one write; the `released` and `after` rows are where a DELETE now differs from a PUT:

```text
taken      it holds the key's lock; rule (1) refused it if its deadline had passed
read       SettleRead on every drive; a drive that does not answer is sent no commit; under N/2 + 1
           answers the write fails with nothing sent
committing each drive is pending, then committed, clear (stale) or still pending (an answer that does
           not say)
success    N/2 + 1 committed: acknowledged, and the key released. Its other commits go on and only add
           copies; each is refused by its stamp once any later commit was applied on its drive
settling   the deadline passed, or every drive answered, short of N/2 + 1: probe each drive not clear,
           which fences the id there, and revert each committed drive
released   a PUT: once no answering drive holds it and the drives that may still hold it (pending,
           running or committed on a host that does not answer) number under N/2
           a DELETE: once no drive may still hold it: none pending, running or committed
           until then requests on the key wait, then fail 503
after      a PUT: a commit that lands later is reverted as it lands, by its own version
           a DELETE: nothing is left to land or to revert
```

A settler (rule (4)) follows the same states. `settleMayRevert` is unchanged: a settler does not revert a write that may have been acknowledged. A drive replaced since its commit went out answers by its new disk and is clear, as today.

Why a PUT keeps its bound and a DELETE does not: a failed PUT's stalled commits each leave a version no read quorum holds, and reverting one restores what its own drive held; they cannot add up with another write's. A failed DELETE's stalled commits leave the one state every DELETE leaves, and a reader counts them together.

**A DELETE that names its object.** A DELETE may carry `x-ur-if-unmodified-ms: T`, the LastModified, in Unix ms, of the object its caller means:

```text
after the key's lock and rule (1), on the object info the handler already reads under the lock
  no object                       as today: nothing is sent to a drive, and the caller gets 204
  ModTime, in ms, >= T + 1,000    412, and nothing is sent to a drive
  else                            the DELETE, by rules (2) and (3)
```

The second of slack lets a caller pass a time it read from a HEAD, whose Last-Modified has whole seconds. `BlobCluster.Delete` sends it for a context that `sidecar.WithBlobUnmodified(ctx, lastModified)` made, as `WithBlobDeadline` carries a deadline today, and answers `ErrBlobPrecondition` on the 412. A DELETE without the header is unconditional, as it is today.

**A LIST that is whole.** MinIO asks the drives of a set that are online and lists a key that at least half of those asked hold (`cmd/metacache-set.go:728-733`). An acknowledged key is on N/2 + 1 drives, so a LIST names every key that can still be read while no drive of the set is offline, or at most two are and none is healing; past that it can drop a key whose shards are only out of reach. The horizon is a LIST, GC's and the container rows' reads of pidx/ are LISTs, and a reader's negative pidx/ lookup is one. The build therefore answers a LIST 503 whenever a set it must read is past that line, and asks every online drive whatever `list_quorum` is set to. That line is §19.6's at_risk state on a metadata set (a third drive lost, or a drive lost during a heal) and one host down on a segment set.

**Settings.** `StampKeep` (`_MINIO_SETTLE_STAMP_KEEP`, 2 min) joins `cmd/settle-settings.go`. Nothing else is new, and `RequestDeadlineMax`, `CommitDeadline` and `StashKeepMinAge` keep their values.

**One build.** A commit's expectation changes form, from `version` to `version@boot:n`, and a drive compares it whole, so a coordinator and a drive of different builds agree on nothing and every commit between them is stale: a mixed cluster fails closed. D-OPS-20's build has run on no cluster, so no upgrade across this change is owed; §19.6's "per build, upgrade and cluster" gate covers later ones.

#### 2.2.3 evs: the record, and the fence of a ref with no head

Three rules. The first two are already what the landed code does and become rules a test holds; the third is a change.

```text
record   an attempt appends its batch record and awaits its write before it issues step 7, and checks
         step 7's 5 s window after that write, against step 4's reads (pushAttempt.commit: step6, then
         withinStepSeven, then HeadStore.Commit). So the record of any attempt whose head write can land
         was acknowledged within 5 s of a 5h check that passed
minute   a batch opens only while the process's clock is sure (§19.6's clocks row), under the UTC minute
         it opens in. So a batch's key names a minute no later than 50 ms past the time each of its
         records joined it
fence    HeadStore.RaiseFence on a ref with no head creates a placeholder head If-None-Match: version 0,
         no window, kind or mode, fence 1, fence_ms its writer's clock. On 412 it reads the head again and
         goes on as after any 412: a commit that landed first is found committed by Resolve, a refusal's
         placeholder is fenced by If-Match
```

The `record` rule binds every route that writes a head naming new segments: a push, a seal, and EVSB-M2-20's re-seed, whose reseed record goes before its head write. The `minute` rule is a change of one check: `BatchWriter` opens a batch only while `ClockCheck.Sure()`, and `Append` answers `ErrEvsClockUnsure` otherwise, which its caller answers 503 as it does any unwritten batch. Push routes already refuse before step 4 on an unsure clock; this closes the attempt that was past step 4 when the clock turned.

A placeholder a fence made is the placeholder a refusal makes (§11.8's first row), with fence_ms set: reads, listings, `GET .../refs` and the lease route treat it as absent; the ref's first commit replaces it by If-Match and keeps its fence count and any refusal records; it stays, as a tombstone head does. A creating attempt that held the absent head fails its If-None-Match, reads the placeholder, finds its fence_ms later than its own arrival and ends 503 unknown, as §11.8's fence row says of any head. An attempt that arrives later reads the placeholder and commits on it by If-Match.

Evacuation's resolve row then needs no case for a ref with no head:

```text
per record, on its ref's head read from the cluster (a held key waits, then 503: the minute waits)
  committed at this place    keep: container, then pidx/ entry, then the batch         (as today)
  committed at another       drop                                                      (as today)
  dead                       drop, with the new slots its record lists                 (as today)
  pending                    RaiseFence, which now always has a head to raise or makes one; resolve again
                             on the head it wrote: dead, by the fence_ms just set, or committed
```

`ResolvePush` needs no change: on a placeholder its first dead rule cannot hold (the version is 0) and its second does (the statement's 35 min are long past at 25 h, and fence_ms is now).

#### 2.2.4 Segment GC by the evacuation horizon

```text
AdoptionBound   24 h + 2 min: the last minute directory that can hold a record adopting a segment starts no
                later than its LastModified + AdoptionBound (2.3's arithmetic)
horizon H       of a metadata cluster, from one LIST of pb/ with limit 1 at time t by the lister's checked
                clock: the start of the minute the oldest batch key names, or t - 25 h, evacuation's floor,
                if that is earlier or no batch is left. Every batch whose minute starts before H has been
                evacuated
orphan          a seg/ object of a repo whose LastModified + AdoptionBound is at or before the H of the
                repo's metadata cluster and whose id no pidx/ entry of the repo lists as introduced
```

Orphan GC runs inside the nightly pass (EVSB-M2-12), per shard job and repo, as P2 work that spends no NVMe budget (its DELETEs are on the HDDs):

```text
shard job, before any LIST of pidx/:
  0  no GC in this job while ClockCheck.Sure() is false, nor for a repo while SettlePassed() is false on the
     segment cluster or on the repo's metadata cluster (§19.6: every host answering, on the build that passed)
  1  H[c] for each metadata cluster c the shard's repos are placed on: one LIST(pb/, limit 1) each, as above

per repo R on metadata cluster c, after the pass's LISTs of seg/<R>/ and pidx/<R>/ (both issued after step 1):
  2  proceed only while repo/<R> shows active or deleted and no hold covers R (each cached at most 5 s)
  3  C := the seg/ objects with H[c] - Window <= LastModified + AdoptionBound <= H[c]; none: done
  4  I := the introduced ids of every pidx/<R>/ entry whose own LastModified is at or after
          min over C of LastModified, less 1 h; each entry by one GET. A 404 on a listed entry (a pack
          replaced its parcel): LIST pidx/<R>/<its ref>/ again and read what was not read, once.
          Over PidxReadCount (4,096) entries: delete nothing for R in this run and alarm
          gc_orphan_index_bound
  5  for each s in C not in I, oldest first, at most DeleteCount (1,024) a repo a run and DeleteRate
     (10 a second) a segment cluster, paused while that cluster's drive operations pass 50% of its measured
     capacity ({nvb_<cluster>}, as a drop job's are):
       step 2's two reads again; a hold or another state ends R's run
       DELETE seg/<R>/<s> with x-ur-if-unmodified-ms: its listed LastModified
         204                       deleted
         412                       the id was uploaded again: a new object, judged on a later night
         503 held, or unknown      left for a later night; never counted as deleted
```

`Window` is 7 d: the pass keeps no cursor (EVSB-M2-12), so each night judges the segments whose bound the horizon passed within the last 7 d, a segment about seven times, and a pass that did not run for longer than that is followed by one run with `Window` set to the gap. `DeleteCount`, `DeleteRate`, `Window` and `PidxReadCount` are `OrphanGcSettings`.

What GC no longer does: it raises no fence, waits no deadline, makes no second check and reads no batch. What it newly needs is `SettlePassed`, which §19.6 already asks of every other job whose DELETE leans on the settle rules: GC's DELETE now leans on rule (3) and on the condition it carries, and its horizon on a LIST that names every acknowledged batch, which 2.2.2's last rule makes the store's promise. Step 1 before step 4 is the one order that matters (twin `GcReadsIndexFirst`): an entry written before a batch's deletion is seen by any LIST issued after an H that the deletion moved.

A kind-5 segment that evacuation writes to seg/ from a batch (EVSB-M10-02's staged decision) is introduced by its record, whose pidx/ entry lists it, and is written in the run that writes that entry; it is a candidate 49 h later at the earliest and is found in I. An uploaded kind-5 segment whose push never committed is an orphan like any other.

#### 2.2.5 Uncommitted path maps

§11.6's map row sends "a map uncommitted 25 h after its upload" to the orphan rule. A PATH_EPOCH push adopts a map only while every part is under 24 h old at its check (5e), so the map's bound is its oldest part's LastModified + AdoptionBound. In the same job, for each `pmap/<R>/<ref>/<p>/<map>/` whose bound is at or before H[c]: read the ref's head from the cluster (after step 1; a held key leaves the map for a later night); if the head's current path epoch is below p, DELETE each part with `x-ur-if-unmodified-ms` its listed LastModified. A map at or below the head's current epoch is left to §11.6's "once p or a newer epoch commits" rule, which knows the committed map. The argument is 2.3's for a segment, with the ref's own head in place of the pidx/ entries: every PATH_EPOCH attempt that could adopt the map has a record behind the horizon, so it committed, and the head read after H shows an epoch at or past p, or it is dead.

#### 2.2.6 What a caller sees

```text
caller                      a held key (503, ErrBlobHeld)                a DELETE's unknown outcome
push, seal, lease           503 {outcome: unknown} once step 7 was       n/a
                            issued, else 503; the client retries
                            (as today)
fold, copy                  the write is retried by the next fold or     n/a
                            the copy's next pass (as today)
evacuation                  the record's minute waits (as today)         the batch is listed again next run
                                                                         and its records resolve as before
marker collection           the marker stays for a later window          the marker is read again in a later
                                                                         window; a 404 is done
versionless purge, sweep    the candidate is left to the sweep, then     the sweep HEADs it again
                            to the next run's sweep
orphan GC                   left for a later night                       left for a later night
drop job                    the id stays unanswered; the cursor does     the id stays unanswered
                            not pass it
a reader of a batch         as a 404 on the batch: the record is         n/a
record                      looked up through pidx/ (RecordLocator)
```

The last row is a change: a batch whose DELETE failed with a commit stalled on a silent host is held, and every record in it was moved before that DELETE was issued (I-EVS-7), so `RecordLocator` treats `ErrBlobHeld` on a pb/ key as it treats a 404: it looks the record up through pidx/, and answers the 503 only if no entry holds it.

### 2.3 Invariants and why they hold

```text
store (Settle.tla)
NoStaleQuorum,       FI-30's first and third clauses: a read returns only the state the store decided, and no
ReadsSeeCurrent      earlier write, revert or heal undoes it
                     why: a write is acknowledged with N/2 + 1 drives holding its state. A drive among them
                     changes afterwards only by a commit that passes rule (2) there, so one whose coordinator
                     read the drive after the acknowledged commit landed on it: never an older write's last
                     commit, whose stamp is spent, and never an older write's revert, which needs the drive
                     still to hold that write. A later PUT leaves its own version there, and its revert puts
                     back what it replaced; a later DELETE leaves absence, acknowledged or reverted before
                     its key is released; a heal copies the state then readable. So an older version, or an
                     older absence, can stand only on the at most N/2 - 1 drives outside that quorum, under a
                     read quorum
LateWritesNeverRead  a PUT released as failed is never read, whatever of it still lands (rule (3), unchanged)
RefusedNeverLands    nothing the store refused past its deadline reaches a drive (rule (1), unchanged)
FailedDeleteSettled  once a failed DELETE's key is released, no drive commit of it can land or be reverted
                     why: rule (3) releases it only with no drive pending, running or committed
HeldKeyReleased      every held key is released once its stalled commits answer and its hosts return (liveness)
                     why: a stalled commit answers committed or stale; a committed one is reverted, by the
                     coordinator or the settler; a write a settler cannot revert, because it may have been
                     acknowledged, is found to hold a write quorum once its hosts answer

evs (EvsGc.tla)
ClosureHolds         I-EVS-1 for segments: no committed head ever names a deleted segment
GcSafe               I-EVS-5: no segment becomes reachable after GC decided to delete it
RecordsKept          I-EVS-2 and I-EVS-7: a committed push's record is in its batch or in a container a pidx/
                     entry names
HeadsRise            a placeholder head exists only with its fence raised
RecordsLeave         every record old enough to evacuate leaves its batch (liveness): none stays pending for
                     want of a head to fence
```

**Why GC is safe.** Let s be a seg/ object with LastModified T, and suppose GC found T + AdoptionBound at or before H, where H came from a LIST of pb/ at time t, and then found s in no pidx/ entry.

1. An attempt can commit a version naming s as new only with a receipt for this object. A fresh receipt's `upload_ms` is evs's clock before the PUT began and a re-upload's is the LastModified itself, so `upload_ms` is at most T + 100 ms. Its last 5h check passed under 24 h after `upload_ms` by evs's clock.
2. By the `record` rule its record was acknowledged within 5 s after such a check, and by the `minute` rule the batch's key names a minute that began no later than 50 ms past that. So the batch was acknowledged before T + 24 h + 5.3 s and its minute began before then too, which is 114.7 s before T + AdoptionBound.
3. H is at most t - 25 h, so the LIST ran a day after T + AdoptionBound, when every such batch had long been acknowledged and so was listed unless deleted (2.2.2's LIST rule). The oldest batch listed begins at or after H. So every such batch has been deleted. A batch whose PUT stalled and lands later holds only records whose attempts were told their batch was not written and issued nothing.
4. Evacuation deletes a batch only after it settled each record (I-EVS-7): kept, with its container and its pidx/ entry, which lists s, written first; dropped as a second copy of a push that another record commits, to which 2 and 3 apply as well; or dead.
5. Dead is final. A pending record's ref is fenced, by a head CAS or, for a ref with no head, by the placeholder's creation. A stalled head write holds the key, so the fence waits behind it and finds it landed, the record then resolving committed, or reverted. Every other attempt of the push that reached evs before the fence holds the head as it was and fails its write, or reads the fenced head and ends (§11.8's fence row); one that arrives later fails 5b, 25 h after its statement's time.
6. So from t on, every push that adopts this object is committed behind a pidx/ entry listing s, or will never commit. GC's LIST and GETs of pidx/ are issued after t, and an entry is never deleted before the entry that replaces it is written (§11.13's index row). Not finding s there, no version names this object and none ever will.
7. A version that names s later carries a receipt from a later upload, which made a new object, since If-None-Match stored it after the old one was gone. Its LastModified is days past T, and a DELETE carrying `x-ur-if-unmodified-ms: T` answers 412 for it. So however late, and however many times, a GC run issues its DELETE, it removes the object it judged or nothing.
8. A version that names s without a receipt took it from a committed version step 4 read (5h), so s was already introduced, and 6 found it.

The margins of step 2 are `EvsGc.tla`'s ASSUME, in ms: 24 h for the receipt, 100 for its stamp against LastModified, 5,000 for step 7's window, 50 for each of two clocks and 60,000 for a key's minute. They sum to 54.8 s less than AdoptionBound.

**Why a forgotten stamp is safe.** A commit c carries the stamp boot:n it read at time r, and its deadline is at most r + 1 min. Suppose a commit c' was applied to the key on that drive after r. While c' is remembered the drive's stamp carries a higher count than any c could have read, so c is stale. Once c' is forgotten, StampKeep after it was applied, the stamp reads boot:0, which equals c's only if c read boot:0; but that is at least 2 min after r, a minute past c's deadline, and the gate refuses c on the drive's clock, which §19.6 holds within 50 ms. After a restart the boot differs and every earlier read is stale.

**The models.** `Settle.tla` is `StoreSettle.tla`, which the data lane owns and this section leaves untouched, with the two store rules. A stamp is the fact `fresh[w][d]`: no commit was applied on drive d since write w's coordinator read it; every commit, revert that changes a drive and heal clears it for every write. A failed DELETE's release needs no drive that may still hold it. A heal's commit is read under the key and may reach its drive after the key's release, as a write's may, where `StoreSettle.tla` checks it in the step that reads. It adds `MaxPuts` and `MaxDeletes`, which fix a run's mix of writes, `Still`, which holds heal or cancels out of a run, the invariant `FailedDeleteSettled`, and the action constraint `NoLateWriteCommits`, which one configuration uses to leave heal's the only late commit. Twin `Written` turns both rules off, which is §19.6 as DESIGN.md states it; `NoStamp` and `DeleteReleasesEarly` turn off one each; `StoreSettle.tla`'s seven twins are kept.

`EvsGc.tla` is new and small where `EvsCommit.tla` is whole: one repo's segments (uploaded, deleted and uploaded again), a ref with a head and a ref with none, pushes that take a receipt, check it, write a batch record and issue a head write that lands, fails, stalls holding its key or is sent late by a paused process, the evacuator (resolve, fence, placeholder, keep, drop, killed at any step), one or two GC runs whose DELETE may itself stall, and time in ticks, where a receipt lasts 2 and a minute is evacuated 3 ticks old. Its twin `Written` is §11.13's orphans row as DESIGN.md states it.

Runs, TLC at the owner's jar (master d8fb231), each bounded so it finishes; breadth-first over every reachable state at its bounds unless it says simulation. `run-settle.sh` stops a run whose state directory passes 8 GB and deletes each run's state directory as it ends; the largest here used 1.7 GB on disk.
